title: Complex Contradictions as Drivers of Expansive Learning in Water Resources Co-management in the uMzimvubu Catchment
text_snippet: Complex Contradictions as Drivers of Expansive Learning in Water Resources Co-management in the uMzimvubu Catchment The aim of this article is to understand complex contradictions which are involved in collaborative management of water resources at a catchment level in South Africa, where numerous water challenges exist including security of supply, degradation of ecological infrastructure, poor landscape governance and resource pollution. To address water related challenges, South Africa has defi ned several Strategic Water Source Areas (SWSAs), one of which is the uMzimvubu catchment in the Eastern Cape. The uMzimvubu catchment is located in the former Transkei homeland, and the river system runs along the northern border of the Eastern Cape Province. The study draws on Cultural History Activity Th eory (CHAT) and it analyses contradictions within and between activity systems in the uMzimvubu catchment. In this theory, contradictions are the source of expansive learning; they are the focus of co-engagement to resolve identifi ed contradictions using formative intervention methodology. Change Laboratories (or Change Labs) were used in this study as hubs for learning and the methodological approach was informed by the expansive learning cycle. title: Emergent Voices and Collective Actions of Environmental Rangers against Peatland Degradation Challenges
text_snippet: Emergent Voices and Collective Actions of Environmental Rangers against Peatland Degradation Challenges Peatland degradation in South Sumatra, Indonesia, has become a critical environmental challenge driven by large-scale agricultural expansion, deforestation, and recurrent fi res, resulting in substantial carbon emissions, biodiversity loss, and socio-economic impacts on local communities. Th is study explores the environmental awareness, motivations and collective actions of high school students actively engaged in student-led and community-based environmental organisations addressing peatland degradation challenges. Employing a qualitative approach, data were collected through in-depth interviews and focus group discussions with 27 students and analysed using thematic analysis. The findings reveal that student environmental rangers develop a multidimensional form of environmental awareness that integrates ecological literacy, emotional attachment to peatland landscapes, and moral responsibility, and this awareness functions as a catalyst for sustained collective action. Th is awareness is translated into concrete initiatives, including environmental education campaigns, peatland restoration activities, and policy-oriented advocacy. title: Development of Sustainable Local Food Economies: A conceptual tool
text_snippet: Development of Sustainable Local Food Economies: A conceptual tool The transition towards sustainable, localised and just food economies requires fundamental structural changes within the skills development system. South Africa’s current skills models remain siloed and inadequate for addressing the food system’s complex social, technical and ecological dynamics. To address this gap, this article draws on the social skills ecosystems framework to develop an integrated mapping tool that examines skills as an enabler between verticalities (policies and hierarchical structures) and horizontalities (collaborative networks and local actor relationships) within local food economies. Th e tool was trialled across three South African case studies in the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng. Initial desktop-based mapping results reveal a systemic bias in regional education and training towards large-scale commercial agriculture, alongside a generic short-course culture lacking clear learning pathways. These models marginalise smallholder farmers and informal traders and provide limited support for sustainable practices such as urban farming and agroecology. title: Pre-service Teachers’ Understandings and Practices of Climate Change
text_snippet: Pre-service Teachers’ Understandings and Practices of Climate Change Globally, climate change (CC) is one of the most critical challenges of the 21st century with far-reaching environmental social, economic and political impacts. Climate change education (CCE) is essential to educate citizens about CC, its eff ects, adaptations, and mitigations, including how lifestyles need to be adjusted. Educators at both schooling and higher education levels therefore should be informed and wellequipped to educate about CC. Pre-service teachers (PSTs) need more exposure to both climate science content and pedagogical content knowledge relating to climate science teaching. Research on how pre-service teachers’ understandings and practices are influenced by their learnings about CC is lacking. Th is study investigated 40 preservice science teachers’ understandings and practices on CC, before and after a Biological Science for Educators module, in a Bachelor of Education undergraduate programme, at a South African university. Th e data generation methods in this qualitative, interpretive study included questionnaires and in-depth individual and focus group interviews. title: Exploring Elements of Social Learning in Local Climate Action Strategies
text_snippet: Exploring Elements of Social Learning in Local Climate Action Strategies Climate change is a global issue that has local impacts. Southern African communities are arguably more vulnerable to the effects of climate change due to limited resources for adaptation and mitigation. This article reports on the results of a study that explores how local climate action strategies promote social learning among community members and the role that social learning plays in climate action. The article draws on social learning elements identified by Fisher et al. (2016) for analysing elements of social learning found in local climate actions. The study used a case study design with an interpretive qualitative approach, involving ten community farmers engaged in climate action initiatives. Using thematic analysis, I identified local climate action initiatives that include communityowned nutritional gardens, farmer field schools, a conservation agriculture (CA) project and collaborative farming extension initiatives. These all exhibited the following social learning elements: 1) participation and mobilisation, 2) knowledge co-production, 3) iterative reflection, and 4) norm and practice revisions. title: Editorial
text_snippet: Editorial Climate change education is at the intersection of power, policy, and pedagogy in a world increasingly defined by intensifying crises (Stevenson et al., 2017). Although climate change is a global phenomenon with widespread impacts, its effects are more pronounced in low-income countries (Gates, 2021), where poverty and limited adaptive capacity exacerbate vulnerability to climate-related risks (Ngcamu, 2023). In recent years, the world has experienced a rise in extreme weather occurrences, including storms, floods, heatwaves, and droughts, which have transformed livelihoods, communities, and learning environments (Nhamo & Chikodzi, 2021). In light of this, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC, 2021) employed the phrase “code red for humanity” to draw attention to the urgency of the climate crisis and to indicate that humanity is already living with the consequences of climate change. These realities require that climate change education transcends a dominant focus on abstract scientific knowledge about climate change, to confront questions of justice, equity, and sustainability (Lotz-Sisitka et al., 2021; Trott et al., 2023). title: Meta-Review of a Collection of Papers: Teacher Education and Future Sustainability - A synthesis of formative research papers towards a Handprint learning action approach to ESD informing teacher education
text_snippet: Meta-Review of a Collection of Papers: Teacher Education and Future Sustainability - A synthesis of formative research papers towards a Handprint learning action approach to ESD informing teacher education Editor’s note: This meta-review of a collection of papers is a fairly unusual paper for the Southern African Journal of Environmental Education. Normally one would have a Book Review as a review paper in a Journal. However, this meta-review is interesting, because it is a collection of papers (see Appendix A) that were compiled by a team of researchers over an extended period of time, as they wrote up the research they were doing to inform a Handbook for Teacher Education. The Handbook entitled Handprints for Change: A teacher education handbook – Activating handprint learning actions in primary schools and beyond was published in 2022 (Sarabhai, Henze, O’Donoghue, Sandoval-Rivera & Shimray, 2022) and is mainly a collaboration between global South partners working in the ESD ExpertNet project (ESD ExpertNet, n.d), produced with German collaboration. A comprehensive and very useful review of this Handbook was recently published in the South African Journal of Science in a piece entitled Activating handprints, not footprints by Caleb Mandikonza (2024). title: An Experiment in Climate Change Education in a Non-Formal Setting: The Carbon Summer School at Science Gallery Bengaluru
text_snippet: An Experiment in Climate Change Education in a Non-Formal Setting: The Carbon Summer School at Science Gallery Bengaluru South Asia is a high-risk region for climate impact yet climate change education (CCE) remains basic and constrained to disciplinary bounds within formal educational institutions. Widespread CCE is necessary for effective mitigation and adaptation strategies and for building a climate-resilient citizenry. In June 2022, Science Gallery Bengaluru organised a four-week interdisciplinary educational programme, entitled Carbon Summer School (CSS), for 19 participants, aged 19-27. The projectbased learning programme connected selected youth with a variety of researchers, practitioners, and community-based organisations. Questionnaires, interviews and direct observation were used to track participants’ learning trajectories. Materials from this intensive curriculum were repurposed for five online self-directed learning courses. These online resources were supplemented with an instructor guide and deployed in formal educational institutions. Finally, an intensive internal and external evaluation process was carried out. title: Editorial: Transforming Education for Sustainable Futures – Views from the Global South
text_snippet: Editorial: Transforming Education for Sustainable Futures – Views from the Global South This Special Issue on Transforming Education for Sustainable Futures (TESF) – with its emphasis on views from the global South has been in process for many years and has taken a considerable amount of time to develop and complete. It started with a UKRI-GCRFfunded three-year research project established as a partnership between the University of Bristol, and three sub-regional hubs in South Africa, Rwanda, Somalia/Somaliland and one in India, for researching Transformative Education for Sustainable Futures. The project, started in 2019, was established as a TESF Network+ that worked with 67 projects over the three-year period spread across the four sub-regional hubs (see www.https://tesf.network). Like many projects at the time, it was disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic, but researchers in the 67 projects all adopted a knowledge production approach to exploring what it means to transform education for sustainable futures.

title: Appropriating Waste into Teaching Learning Materials for Early Childhood Education – A Sustainability Starts with Teachers approach
text_snippet: Appropriating Waste into Teaching Learning Materials for Early Childhood Education – A Sustainability Starts with Teachers approach Children’s early development socially, emotionally and cognitively is tied to how they are taught and how they learn in tangible ways. The learning experiences in their early years have a significant impact on their general and optimal development. Early childhood is the most critical period of a person’s life in terms of thinking and cognition. Thus, teaching and learning processes need to be innovative with inspiring materials in teacher development programmes. There is a dire shortage of teaching and learning materials in teacher education institutions in Botswana. Using a case study of a teacher education institution in Botswana, the purpose of this article is to demonstrate how an active learning model can be used drawing on a change project approach to respond to the shortage of teaching learning materials (TLMs) for Early Childhood Education (ECE) using waste materials. The change project emerged from a UNESCO-led capacity building programme for teacher educators on Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) in Southern Africa called Sustainability Starts with Teachers (SST). title: Higher Education Engagements with Cities and Sustainability in Northeast India
text_snippet: Higher Education Engagements with Cities and Sustainability in Northeast India This article offers an exploratory analysis of higher education institutions’ engagement with cities and sustainability in Northeast India. The study uses interviews with universities to map various educational institutions and their curricula on sustainability and urbanisation. Five approaches to teaching sustainable urbanisation are identified and relevant research topics, workshops and seminars are discussed. The study finds limitations in teaching and research interventions within higher education curricula in Northeast India, particularly in addressing themes of cities, sustainability and urbanisation, underscoring the need for strengthening outreach, stakeholder consultancy, and public collaboration to keep universities connected to the region’s contemporary and emerging environmental realities. Additionally, the article highlights how several actors outside formal academia, including civil societies, churches and citizen initiatives, contribute to addressing issues of sustainability and urbanisation across various urban centres of Northeast India. title: Exploring the Development of Teachers’ Personal Pedagogical Content Knowledge about Climate Change Education during a Continuing Teacher Professional Development Course
text_snippet: Exploring the Development of Teachers’ Personal Pedagogical Content Knowledge about Climate Change Education during a Continuing Teacher Professional Development Course Climate Change Education (CCE) is widely recognised as one of the effective strategies for mitigating climate change challenges and risks. However, lack of the necessary knowledge and pedagogical skills among the majority of teachers in South Africa hinders its successful implementation at classroom level. To address this issue, we designed and implemented a short course in CCE for a group of high school Geography and Natural Sciences (NS) teachers in the Nelson Mandela Metropolitan district in the Eastern Cape. This article reports on a case study that we conducted to explore the development of the teachers’ personal pedagogical content knowledge (pPCK) about CCE during the course. We also sought to gain insight into the factors that could have supported (amplifiers) or hindered (filters) the development of the teachers’ pPCK about CCE during the course. The study was interpretivist in its approach and used the refined consensus model (RCM) of PCK as its conceptual and analytical framework. The study sample consisted of three purposefully selected NS teachers. Data on the teachers’ pPCK about CCE before and after the course were generated from pre-course and post-course interviews

title: Tree Planting in Semi-Arid Urban Areas: Lessons from Somalia
text_snippet: Tree Planting in Semi-Arid Urban Areas: Lessons from Somalia This article is based on ‘Green Garowe’, a tree planting action research project that was conducted in the drought-affected city of Garowe, Puntland state, Somalia. The project embraced a co-production approach that called for collaboration between the local government of Garowe, community members and Puntland State University researchers. A qualitative research approach was adopted with a tree-planting demonstration that enabled the research team to develop a holistic understanding of the enablers and constraints to tree planting in the city of Garowe. The findings revealed that tree planting in the city of Garowe was low due to social, ecological, climatic and economic conditions. The study also revealed that Garowe had a high tree deficit, necessitating the planting of 90 000 trees by the year 2030. Evidence from the tree planting demonstration revealed that trees can grow in semi-arid urban areas like Garowe with a success rate of over 90% only if they are taken care of and well protected. title: Weaving Science into Creative Writing: Integrating interdisciplinarity into young adult learning
text_snippet: Weaving Science into Creative Writing: Integrating interdisciplinarity into young adult learning Science education and science communication, driven by their shared overarching objectives of awareness, engagement, and comprehension, have gained further potency through the integration of creative forms of expression. Creative methods of expression, particularly creative writing, can make science accessible, relatable, and engaging, which helps promote a scientifically enlightened society. The weaving of scientific concepts and creative writing is crucial in addressing global issues such as climate change. This study investigates the impact of a 12-week science-focused creative writing workshop held in Bangalore, India. The study pays attention to how participants creatively expressed their expanded understanding of the role of carbon and carbon dioxide emissions in influencing climate change. In this qualitative study, we utilised a multi-method approach, which allows for the use of open-ended surveys, assessment of the produced works, and self-assessment processes as ways of gaining insight into how the workshop has inspired participants to integrate science concepts into diverse creative writing genres. title: Integration of Climate Change Concepts in the Namibian School Curriculum: Challenges, opportunities and recommendations for enhanced implementation
text_snippet: Integration of Climate Change Concepts in the Namibian School Curriculum: Challenges, opportunities and recommendations for enhanced implementation Like many countries in the Global South, Namibia is vulnerable to disproportionate impacts of climate change. The country is facing intensified challenges in adapting to rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, and a higher prevalence of extreme weather events, which contribute to existing socio-economic and environmental problems. The complex nature of climate change science requires that climate change concepts are integrated into all education systems. This article is a content analysis of how the Namibian basic education curriculum integrates concepts related to climate change. The analysis reveals that climate change concepts are partially integrated into Namibia’s basic education curriculum as part of the environmental learning cross-curricular theme. This integration of climate change concepts is only evident in the Natural and Social Science subjects across grade levels and mostly covers basic concepts related to climate science, sustainable lifestyles and ecosystems and biodiversity. title: Choosing a Social Learning Theory to Evaluate Farmer-Led Climate Action Networks: A reflective perspective
text_snippet: Choosing a Social Learning Theory to Evaluate Farmer-Led Climate Action Networks: A reflective perspective This article shares my explorations in the search for a social learning theory that could serve as an analytic framework for my research on climate change learning among small-scale women farmers. It also highlights and addresses the concerns of several leading scholars on the lack of clarity and coherence in the articulation of the concept of social learning. Using a theoretical review, adapted from the critical literature review approach, the study traces the origins of three strands of social learning and explores their similarities, diff erences, and relevance in varying contexts. The review found that despite diff erences in disciplinary orientation, all three strands seek to explain the learning relationship between people and their environment. Th e split-off point for the three strands is the conceptualisation of learning and the role of the learner and their environment in shaping the learning process and outcomes. Th rough my exploration, I ultimately identified and adopted the social learning theory rooted in the more recent conceptualisation of Lave and Wenger’s (1991) concept of communities of practice as more aligned with my research question and purpose. title: Towards Change-Oriented Sustainability Education in Teacher Education in Malawi
text_snippet: Towards Change-Oriented Sustainability Education in Teacher Education in Malawi The Berlin Declaration on Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) asserted the essence of mainstreaming ESD in teacher education to provide strategies for policymakers, educators and institutions aiming to advance sustainability through professional development. This study explored the mainstreaming of ESD in teacher education through Vygotsky’s social learning theory and a qualitative research design. Th e study examined the experiences of eight teacher educators from a Malawian teacher training college who participated in UNESCO’s Sustainability Starts with Teachers (SST) programme. The study questioned how the SST initiative could be scaled or adapted to diverse educational contexts towards change-oriented sustainability education in teacher education. Data was generated through a roundtable discussion and analysed using thematic analysis. The findings revealed six key themes: (1) Social issues, highlighting the imperative to confront societal challenges through ESD; (2) Agency, focusing on empowering teacher educators to lead the mainstreaming of ESD; (3) Collaboration, stressing the value of building partnerships among educators and key stakeholders; (4) Historical learnin

title: Using a Field Trip with Biology Students to Study Wetland Ecosystem Birds
text_snippet: Using a Field Trip with Biology Students to Study Wetland Ecosystem Birds Wetlands ecosystems in Lesotho are signifi cant for their rich biodiversity of birds and other species, yet citizens have limited knowledge about their value, and wetlands are faced with destructive anthropogenic pressures. This study investigated the effectiveness of using a field trip with Grade 11 biology students to study local wetland ecosystem birds. Three questions guided the study: “What is the Grade 11 biology students’ knowledge of birds found in Pitseng wetland ecosystem?”; “How does Grade 11 students’ knowledge of birds in Pitseng wetland develop with the use of the field trip approach over time?” and “What is the difference between male and female students’ knowledge of wetland birds, if any?” Using ecological literacy as a theoretical framework, a case study design, in the form of an Action Research method, was employed to answer the research questions. Data was generated using an openended questionnaire and fieldwork observations. The participants were 34 biology students. The analysis of data was both qualitative and quantitative. title: Identifying the Key Behaviours to Promote Sustainable Constructions in Nigeria: A Principal Component Analysis
text_snippet: Identifying the Key Behaviours to Promote Sustainable Constructions in Nigeria: A Principal Component Analysis The burgeoning field of sustainable construction necessitates a profound reevaluation of traditional building practices, with a transition towards eco-friendly, energy-efficient, and socially responsible methodologies in building construction. We studied a unique population of students in Building Technology Education (BTE) whose bi-directional training makes them relevant for environmental education both in classrooms and in actual building construction. We conveniently surveyed 171 students and 47 building construction experts using a 29-item questionnaire. “Restoring brownfi elds for low-cost habitable buildings” and “retraining manpower in sustainable methods” ranked highest in the Relative Importance Index. Validity checks confirmed participant sufficiency, and Principal Component Analysis revealed seven themed components: support for the local economy, manpower and social norms; value for humans and nature; reducing resource consumption and waste generation; use of integrated design approach and building site assessment; recycling and reusing of materials; attention to land use; and incremental green technology integration. title: Lessons Learned from Developing a Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) to Support Citizen Scientists in Africa
text_snippet: Lessons Learned from Developing a Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) to Support Citizen Scientists in Africa Data gaps limit solutions and policy development for environmental issues. Citizen science offers a possible solution to reduce data gaps at a limited cost while enhancing environmental education (EE). While highly effective in the latter, citizen science campaigns rarely produce reliable, comparable, and meaningful data. This often results from fragmented awareness, varying data collection methods, and little training prior to data collection. This article explores how Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) can be used to train citizen scientists, increase the value of citizen science data, and ensure that resources invested in citizen science initiatives are used more efficiently. We use a beach macrolitter monitoring course developed by Sustainable Seas Trust (SST) (NGO/NPO) and GRID-Arendal (a research foundation) as a case study in Africa, since the marine litter issue has widespread public support, and beaches are pleasant locations that attract potential citizen scientists. Beach macrolitter surveys utilise everyday equipment, and monitoring methods are simple if individuals are supported with appropriate training. title: Fostering Students’ Engagement in Low-Carbon Education through an Electricity-Saving Project
text_snippet: Fostering Students’ Engagement in Low-Carbon Education through an Electricity-Saving Project Emissions of carbon dioxide (CO₂) result from burning fossil fuels. Industrial activities continue to produce CO₂, which can increase by up to 64% annually. CO₂ raises global temperatures; this has adverse eff ects on the climate, leading to climate change. In Indonesia, 56% of electricity is generated using coal-fi red power plants, a process that signifi cantly contributes to CO₂ emissions through coal combustion. Consequently, optimising electricity usage is paramount to mitigating these emissions effectively. Reducing emissions is one way to address climate change. Therefore, this study aims to ascertain how university students implement and respond to project-based electricity saving. This case study involved 75 participants enrolled in the Statistics Department. The findings demonstrated that students could complete the one-month project electricity saving (kWh), resulting in reductions in emissions of CO₂ (kg) and developing as sense of Quantitative Literacy (QL). The most popular ways to save electricity are to turn off lights and televisions, unplug phone chargers, use LED lighting, and control the use of electrical fans. title: On the Transformative Potential of Ecopedagogy in Environmental Education
text_snippet: On the Transformative Potential of Ecopedagogy in Environmental Education Amidst mounting environmental crises, achieving sustainability emerges as a paramount imperative for both humanity and the planet. Th is article explores the crucial role of environmental education in fostering sustainable practices on Earth, with a specific focus on the transformative potential of ecopedagogy. It argues that existing educational systems signifi cantly hinder sustainability efforts by perpetuating principles and values that endorse unsustainable lifestyles driven by neoliberalist ideology. Drawing on contemporary research and theoretical frameworks, the article investigates how ecopedagogy can cultivate ecological literacy and instil a transformative ethos among learners. It advocates for a comprehensive overhaul of environmental education by examining prevailing educational paradigms that reinforce unsustainable behaviours. Through critical analysis and dialectical inquiry, ecopedagogy offers a pathway to deeper comprehension of the intricate connections between social conflicts and environmental degradation, paving the way for innovative solutions. title: Trends, Focus Areas and Research Gaps of Doctoral Degrees in Environmental Studies Departments at South African Universities: 1998-2017
text_snippet: Trends, Focus Areas and Research Gaps of Doctoral Degrees in Environmental Studies Departments at South African Universities: 1998-2017 Doctoral research must be original, creative or innovative and must make a significant contribution at the frontiers of a discipline. This article documents the contribution of 19 years of PhD research at six comprehensive and eleven traditional South African universities and identifies research topics through using a systematic literature review method. Two hundred and fourteen (214) environmental studies were scanned, manually and digitally analysed using Leximancer© to identify each PhD’s research theme. Results of what the PhDs focussed on were placed in a corresponding theme under each university. The combination of the number of completed PhDs per theme, the research focus areas and the SARChI research chairs of universities provide guidance to specific future research areas at the universities. Waste management, coastal/marine, mining-related environmental concerns, and protected areas are the broad themes with research potential. These gaps have been identified because few PhDs focused on these issues. title: A Reflective Exploration of an Integrative Approach to Teaching Climate Change and Sustainable Development: A mediated flipped classroom design
text_snippet: A Reflective Exploration of an Integrative Approach to Teaching Climate Change and Sustainable Development: A mediated flipped classroom design Climate change is arguably a complex issue that is affecting different forms and aspects of life on Earth. Climate change challenges manifest as ‘wicked problems’. They also manifest as development concerns impacting socio-ecological systems through extreme weather events that include tornados, severe storms and ensuing floods, high temperatures and droughts. This requires inclusive and holistic knowledge of climate change and its relationship to other development concerns, such as those represented by the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This way of coming to understand climate change can potentially assist students to develop capacity for addressing locally experienced climate change risks and impacts. In the past, I taught climate change, biodiversity, and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in isolation which tended to make students see these as isolated rather than relational concepts. This enquiry into my own teaching and mediation practice, seeks to respond to this problem. title: A Place-Based and Systems Approach to Curriculum Design for Water Education: A case study from Pune, India
text_snippet: A Place-Based and Systems Approach to Curriculum Design for Water Education: A case study from Pune, India Addressing complex socio-environmental challenges such as climate change and ecological degradation is one of the major challenges facing us today. Such challenges cannot be adequately addressed by scientific and technical fixes alone but require a critical assessment of values and priorities implicit in decision-making regarding socio-environmental problems. To develop in school students the knowledge, concepts and skills required to address such challenges, a learning progression called Water Classrooms was developed. Qualitative and semi-quantitative analysis of the activities conducted during Water Classrooms shows that such a pedagogy can indeed enable students to think about water-related issues from physical, cultural and social lenses. Water Classrooms provides a practical example of how multiple stakeholders can co-create an engaging and multidisciplinary curriculum on water that can be adapted to other parts of the world. title: Virtual learning networks for sustainable co-engaged knowledge dissemination.
text_snippet: Virtual learning networks for sustainable co-engaged knowledge dissemination. Learning Networks in the agri-environmental education sector have proven to be a valuable tool for sharing knowledge and building capacity outside formal training processes. During the Covid-19 pandemic, many in-person learning networks transformed into Virtual Learning Networks. Subsequently, it appears that some of these Learning Networks thrive while others die quietly. This paper investigates the elements, functioning and mechanisms of four learning networks in a virtual space to understand what factors contribute to the sustainability of such networks and identify what actions might improve the chances for future success.We drew upon Cultural Historical Activity Theory and developed a contextual profile for each learning network as an activity system. Data was obtained through the use of a Social network mapping tool, WhatsApp Network Group Chat Analysis and interviewed 25 learning network members.The research aimed to understand the functioning, elements and mechanisms of Virtual Learning Networks in order to develop the understandings, approaches and tools necessary to increase the chances of future success for these social knowledge-sharing platforms. The study questioned how the SST initiative could be scaled or adapted to diverse educational contexts towards change-oriented sustainability education in teacher education. Data was generated through a roundtable discussion and analysed using thematic analysis. The findings revealed six key themes: (1) Social issues, highlighting the imperative to confront societal challenges through ESD; (2) Agency, focusing on empowering teacher educators to lead the mainstreaming of ESD; (3) Collaboration, stressing the value of building partnerships among educators and key stakeholders; (4) Historical learnin

title: Higher Education Engagements with Cities and Sustainability in Northeast India
text_snippet: Higher Education Engagements with Cities and Sustainability in Northeast India This article offers an exploratory analysis of higher education institutions’ engagement with cities and sustainability in Northeast India. The study uses interviews with universities to map various educational institutions and their curricula on sustainability and urbanisation. Five approaches to teaching sustainable urbanisation are identified and relevant research topics, workshops and seminars are discussed. The study finds limitations in teaching and research interventions within higher education curricula in Northeast India, particularly in addressing themes of cities, sustainability and urbanisation, underscoring the need for strengthening outreach, stakeholder consultancy, and public collaboration to keep universities connected to the region’s contemporary and emerging environmental realities. Additionally, the article highlights how several actors outside formal academia, including civil societies, churches and citizen initiatives, contribute to addressing issues of sustainability and urbanisation across various urban centres of Northeast India. It highlights the potential of such interventions to complement academic efforts towards sustainable urban development. The artic

title: Meta-Review of a Collection of Papers: Teacher Education and Future Sustainability - A synthesis of formative research papers towards a Handprint learning action approach to ESD informing teacher education
text_snippet: Meta-Review of a Collection of Papers: Teacher Education and Future Sustainability - A synthesis of formative research papers towards a Handprint learning action approach to ESD informing teacher education Editor’s note: This meta-review of a collection of papers is a fairly unusual paper for the Southern African Journal of Environmental Education. Normally one would have a Book Review as a review paper in a Journal. However, this meta-review is interesting, because it is a collection of papers (see Appendix A) that were compiled by a team of researchers over an extended period of time, as they wrote up the research they were doing to inform a Handbook for Teacher Education. The Handbook entitled Handprints for Change: A teacher education handbook – Activating handprint learning actions in primary schools and beyond was published in 2022 (Sarabhai, Henze, O’Donoghue, Sandoval-Rivera & Shimray, 2022) and is mainly a collaboration between global South partners working in the ESD ExpertNet project (ESD ExpertNet, n.d), produced with German collaboration. A comprehensive and very useful review of this Handbook was recently published in the South African Journal of Science in a piece entitled Activating handprints, not footprints by Caleb Mandikonza (2024). Readers can download the Handbook, and the Review of the Handbook (see reference list), and then read this review of the papers

title: Going into Extra Time: Experiences of Knowledge Co-Creation in a Multi-stakeholder Research Partnership in Rwandan Eco-schools
text_snippet: Going into Extra Time: Experiences of Knowledge Co-Creation in a Multi-stakeholder Research Partnership in Rwandan Eco-schools This article uses co-creative reflexive dialogue to explore an experience of using knowledge co-creation as a research methodology in six Rwandan Eco-Schools. By exploring some of the expected and unexpected dynamics, challenges and opportunities, this research aims to contribute new insights into knowledge cocreation for Education for Sustainable Development (ESD). The article provides a rationale, as well as some principles and pitfalls of knowledge co-creation, before presenting an analysis of co-reflexive dialogue between the original research team members regarding their co-creative experience. The findings of the research reveal time to be the single biggest disrupting element in the knowledge co-creation experience. This was apparent from the very beginning and manifested in several different ways throughout the knowledge co-creation process. The relationship between the availability of time, motive for participation, and stakes of the different actors in the success or failure of the research, emerge as justice considerations within the findings ultimately calling for a commitment of all partners to the transformative aims of the research, even beyond the funder timeframe.

title: An Experiment in Climate Change Education in a Non-Formal Setting: The Carbon Summer School at Science Gallery Bengaluru
text_snippet: An Experiment in Climate Change Education in a Non-Formal Setting: The Carbon Summer School at Science Gallery Bengaluru South Asia is a high-risk region for climate impact yet climate change education (CCE) remains basic and constrained to disciplinary bounds within formal educational institutions. Widespread CCE is necessary for effective mitigation and adaptation strategies and for building a climate-resilient citizenry. In June 2022, Science Gallery Bengaluru organised a four-week interdisciplinary educational programme, entitled Carbon Summer School (CSS), for 19 participants, aged 19-27. The projectbased learning programme connected selected youth with a variety of researchers, practitioners, and community-based organisations. Questionnaires, interviews and direct observation were used to track participants’ learning trajectories. Materials from this intensive curriculum were repurposed for five online self-directed learning courses. These online resources were supplemented with an instructor guide and deployed in formal educational institutions. Finally, an intensive internal and external evaluation process was carried out. title: Fostering Students’ Engagement in Low-Carbon Education through an Electricity-Saving Project
text_snippet: Fostering Students’ Engagement in Low-Carbon Education through an Electricity-Saving Project Emissions of carbon dioxide (CO₂) result from burning fossil fuels. Industrial activities continue to produce CO₂, which can increase by up to 64% annually. CO₂ raises global temperatures; this has adverse eff ects on the climate, leading to climate change. In Indonesia, 56% of electricity is generated using coal-fi red power plants, a process that signifi cantly contributes to CO₂ emissions through coal combustion. Consequently, optimising electricity usage is paramount to mitigating these emissions effectively. Reducing emissions is one way to address climate change. Therefore, this study aims to ascertain how university students implement and respond to project-based electricity saving. This case study involved 75 participants enrolled in the Statistics Department. The findings demonstrated that students could complete the one-month project electricity saving (kWh), resulting in reductions in emissions of CO₂ (kg) and developing as sense of Quantitative Literacy (QL). The most popular ways to save electricity are to turn off lights and televisions, unplug phone chargers, use LED lighting, and control the use of electrical fans. title: A Place-Based and Systems Approach to Curriculum Design for Water Education: A case study from Pune, India
text_snippet: A Place-Based and Systems Approach to Curriculum Design for Water Education: A case study from Pune, India Addressing complex socio-environmental challenges such as climate change and ecological degradation is one of the major challenges facing us today. Such challenges cannot be adequately addressed by scientific and technical fixes alone but require a critical assessment of values and priorities implicit in decision-making regarding socio-environmental problems. To develop in school students the knowledge, concepts and skills required to address such challenges, a learning progression called Water Classrooms was developed. Qualitative and semi-quantitative analysis of the activities conducted during Water Classrooms shows that such a pedagogy can indeed enable students to think about water-related issues from physical, cultural and social lenses. Water Classrooms provides a practical example of how multiple stakeholders can co-create an engaging and multidisciplinary curriculum on water that can be adapted to other parts of the world. title: Appropriating Waste into Teaching Learning Materials for Early Childhood Education – A Sustainability Starts with Teachers approach
text_snippet: Appropriating Waste into Teaching Learning Materials for Early Childhood Education – A Sustainability Starts with Teachers approach Children’s early development socially, emotionally and cognitively is tied to how they are taught and how they learn in tangible ways. The learning experiences in their early years have a significant impact on their general and optimal development. Early childhood is the most critical period of a person’s life in terms of thinking and cognition. Thus, teaching and learning processes need to be innovative with inspiring materials in teacher development programmes. There is a dire shortage of teaching and learning materials in teacher education institutions in Botswana. Using a case study of a teacher education institution in Botswana, the purpose of this article is to demonstrate how an active learning model can be used drawing on a change project approach to respond to the shortage of teaching learning materials (TLMs) for Early Childhood Education (ECE) using waste materials. title: Integration of Climate Change Concepts in the Namibian School Curriculum: Challenges, opportunities and recommendations for enhanced implementation
text_snippet: Integration of Climate Change Concepts in the Namibian School Curriculum: Challenges, opportunities and recommendations for enhanced implementation Like many countries in the Global South, Namibia is vulnerable to disproportionate impacts of climate change. The country is facing intensified challenges in adapting to rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, and a higher prevalence of extreme weather events, which contribute to existing socio-economic and environmental problems. The complex nature of climate change science requires that climate change concepts are integrated into all education systems. This article is a content analysis of how the Namibian basic education curriculum integrates concepts related to climate change. The analysis reveals that climate change concepts are partially integrated into Namibia’s basic education curriculum as part of the environmental learning cross-curricular theme. This integration of climate change concepts is only evident in the Natural and Social Science subjects across grade levels and mostly covers basic concepts related to climate science, sustainable lifestyles and ecosystems and biodiversity. title: Trends, Focus Areas and Research Gaps of Doctoral Degrees in Environmental Studies Departments at South African Universities: 1998-2017
text_snippet: Trends, Focus Areas and Research Gaps of Doctoral Degrees in Environmental Studies Departments at South African Universities: 1998-2017 Doctoral research must be original, creative or innovative and must make a significant contribution at the frontiers of a discipline. This article documents the contribution of 19 years of PhD research at six comprehensive and eleven traditional South African universities and identifies research topics through using a systematic literature review method. Two hundred and fourteen (214) environmental studies were scanned, manually and digitally analysed using Leximancer© to identify each PhD’s research theme. Results of what the PhDs focussed on were placed in a corresponding theme under each university. The combination of the number of completed PhDs per theme, the research focus areas and the SARChI research chairs of universities provide guidance to specific future research areas at the universities. Waste management, coastal/marine, mining-related environmental concerns, and protected areas are the broad themes with research potential. These gaps have been identified because few PhDs focused on these issues. title: Editorial
text_snippet: Editorial Climate change education is at the intersection of power, policy, and pedagogy in a world increasingly defined by intensifying crises (Stevenson et al., 2017). Although climate change is a global phenomenon with widespread impacts, its effects are more pronounced in low-income countries (Gates, 2021), where poverty and limited adaptive capacity exacerbate vulnerability to climate-related risks (Ngcamu, 2023). In recent years, the world has experienced a rise in extreme weather occurrences, including storms, floods, heatwaves, and droughts, which have transformed livelihoods, communities, and learning environments (Nhamo & Chikodzi, 2021). In light of this, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC, 2021) employed the phrase “code red for humanity” to draw attention to the urgency of the climate crisis and to indicate that humanity is already living with the consequences of climate change. These realities require that climate change education transcends a dominant focus on abstract scientific knowledge about climate change, to confront questions of justice, equity, and sustainability (Lotz-Sisitka et al., 2021; Trott et al., 2023). title: Using a Field Trip with Biology Students to Study Wetland Ecosystem Birds
text_snippet: Using a Field Trip with Biology Students to Study Wetland Ecosystem Birds Wetlands ecosystems in Lesotho are signifi cant for their rich biodiversity of birds and other species, yet citizens have limited knowledge about their value, and wetlands are faced with destructive anthropogenic pressures. This study investigated the effectiveness of using a field trip with Grade 11 biology students to study local wetland ecosystem birds.
